title: Six weeks off
text:
Marina had never missed a training session in two years. Then, in the last ten minutes of an ordinary Tuesday game, she sprained her ankle.

The physiotherapist was direct. Six weeks, no running. She could swim after week two, and lift weights with her upper body from the start.

The first ten days were the worst. Not the pain, the boredom. She watched her team play twice from the side and left early both times.

What changed her mood was a small decision. Instead of counting the days until she could run, she set a different target: get stronger in the parts of her body she had ignored for years. She trained her shoulders and back three times a week and kept a note of every session.

By week five she was swimming 1,500 metres without stopping, something she couldn't do before the injury.

She came back in October and ran a personal best in her first 10K two months later. Her coach said the rest had done what training couldn't.

Marina put it differently. She said the injury taught her that a rest day is part of the plan, not a break from it.

questions.q: What did she find hardest at first?
What did she do instead of waiting to run again?
options: Trained the parts of her body she had ignored

questions.q: What did Marina learn from the injury?
options: Rest is part of training, not a break from it
Running is bad for the ankles

title: The underdogs
text:
Before the final, every newspaper picked the same winner. The favourites had beaten our team twice that season, once 4-0.

The coach didn't argue with any of it. In the team talk he said one sentence: "They have to win. We only have to play."

We were the underdogs and everyone knew it, including us. The strange thing is that it helped. There was no pressure in the changing room, only a kind of curiosity.

They scored first, after eleven minutes. At half-time we were 1-0 down and, honestly, lucky it wasn't three.

The second half was different. Their captain was sent off for a foul near the halfway line, and suddenly the game had a shape we could use. We equalised in the 70th minute and the stadium, mostly their supporters, went quiet.

It went to extra time. Nobody scored. Then penalties, which are less about skill than about who can breathe.

We won 4-3. Our goalkeeper, who had said almost nothing all season, saved two.

Home advantage, better players, better league position. None of it mattered for one afternoon.

questions.q: Why was the team called the underdogs?
What changed the shape of the game?
options: The opposing captain was sent off

questions.q: How was the match finally decided?
What point does the last line make?
